extracted.intended_audience: labor/employment lawyers, employers, unions, rulemaking stakeholders, and agency adjudicators involved in NLRB joint-employer rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and application guidance for the NLRB's joint-employer standard under the NLRA, including threshold common-law employment requirements, what counts as control over essential terms and conditions, and associated bargaining and procedural obligations. Discusses examples (work rules, contracts, surveillance, health and safety), burden of proof, and recusal/conflict-of-interest standards for rule participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold common-law employment relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: General contractors (or any entity) will be deemed joint employers only if all requirements of the standard are established, including the threshold requirement that they have a common-law employment relationship with particular employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule emphasizes performing the required threshold analysis consistent with the common law so that entities with highly attenuated relationships to particular employees are not deemed joint employers. The phrase 'tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge' is used to encompass actions that determine or alter individuals' employment status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure of employment (including hiring and discharge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board uses the phrase 'tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge' to encompass a range of actions that determine or alter individuals' employment status, offering hiring and discharge as examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrase signals that control over who is hired/fired or other tenure-related actions is central to establishing a common-law employment relationship for joint-employer analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential terms and conditions of employment must be identified
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board must 'explain which terms and conditions are `essential' to permit `meaningful collective bargaining,' and to 'clarify what `meaningful collective bargaining' entails and how it works in this setting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing an (exhaustive) list of essential terms and conditions responds to court guidance and frames what will be subject to joint-employer scrutiny and potential bargaining obligations. The Board reformatted §103.40(e) and §103.40(c) to address this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over essential terms must permit meaningful collective bargaining
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiry into 'whether the putative joint employer possesses sufficient control over employees' essential terms and conditions of employment to permit meaningful collective bargaining' (the BFI second element) is applied in the rule via §103.40(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although that 'meaningful collective bargaining' step was self-imposed in BFI, the final rule examines whether the character and objects of a purported employer's control extend to essential terms within the Act's context, per D.C. Circuit guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work rules and directions as indicators of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Work rules or directions may be especially clear indicators of a putative joint employer's authority to control or exercise control over the details of particular employees' work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will consider concrete examples (e.g., maintenance of `workflow training charts') as probative of control. Work rules that clearly govern employees' performance can support a joint-employer finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous work-rule language not automatically determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board rejects the suggestion it will seize upon ambiguous language in work rules to make a joint-employer finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous wording alone will not be treated as dispositive; the Board looks for meaningful indicators of authority or exercise of control rather than relying on ambiguous or vague rule language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace health and safety can be an essential term
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board believes that 'the physical conduct' of an employee 'in the performance of the service' to the employer encompasses workplace health and safety, and thus health and safety may be regarded as an essential term or condition of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule does not prescribe specific substantive health and safety standards (recognizing other agencies' expertise), and a contract term that simply memorializes an employer's choice about how to comply with regulations would not indicate joint-employer status; but reserved authority or discretion over health and safety matters would bear on the inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between memorialized compliance and reserved/control over safety
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employer's compliance with health and safety regulations involves choosing among alternative methods, a contract term that merely memorializes the employer's choice does not indicate joint-employer status; however, reserved further authority or discretion over health and safety matters, or control exercised pursuant to such a reservation, would bear on the joint-employer inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether contractual language confers actual retained decisionmaking power (probative of control) versus merely documenting compliance obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract provisions and contracting regimes as evidence of indirect control
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract terms, standard-form contracting documents (e.g., AIA Document A201-2017), Federal Acquisition Regulation provisions, cost-plus contracting, and other contract provisions can memorialize duties and obligations and may be probative of a user's indirect control over supplier employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some provisions (e.g., cost-plus contracting) have been identified as potentially probative of indirect control over wages; other contracting rules (TSA, UIIA, marine terminal rules) may define terms and conditions relevant to the inquiry. Provisions that only memorialize compliance with legal minimums are less likely material to common-law employment relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveillance and other indirect mechanisms may demonstrate control
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveillance has been suggested as a mechanism that, in certain contexts, might demonstrate sufficient indirect control over employees' essential terms and conditions to justify a joint-employer finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters raised surveillance as relevant; the Board indicated it would consider whether such mechanisms, in context, establish joint-employer status, though they did not propose modifying the rule specifically to add surveillance language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular and continuous control versus sporadic/de minimis control
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters argue the Board should require a showing of regular and continuous control (not merely sporadic and de minimis control) to find joint-employer status; some urged incorporating a de minimis limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule and its application must address the degree, frequency, and continuity of control necessary to support a joint-employer finding; commenters disagree about where to draw the line.

rubrics_metrics.name: When employer discretion over statutory compliance exists, bargaining is required
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employer has discretion over how to comply with a statutory mandate, it must bargain about how to exercise that discretion (e.g., how to satisfy confidentiality obligations while meeting NLRA duties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited precedent (Roseburg Forest Products Co.) requires bargaining with the union over how the employer will exercise discretion to comply with other legal obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects bargaining obligations when subcontracting or terminating relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate whether an employer must bargain under Sec. 8(a)(5) before terminating a relationship with a subcontractor or other business entity; some urge the Board to require expedited effects bargaining when contractual changes affect employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board notes differing precedents (e.g., Malbaff) and commenter positions; the timing and scope of bargaining obligations for subcontracting/termination are fact-specific and may be addressed by adjudication or expedited bargaining in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof assignment and APA/vagueness concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters contend the proposed rule is too vague about how a party carries its burden and that this could violate the Administrative Procedure Act; others note the APA requires the Board to assign the burden of proof as proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board discusses these contentions and explains that assigning the burden of proof in the rule is consistent with APA requirements; clarity in articulating the burden and how it is to be carried is important to avoid procedural challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of common-law agency principles, including reserved and indirect control
rubrics_metrics.description: The District of Columbia Circuit emphasized that failure to consider reserved or indirect control is inconsistent with the common law of agency; the Board will be guided by the court's treatment in applying the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will address whether mechanisms that grant third parties control over particular employees' terms and conditions establish joint-employer status in adjudication, using common-law agency principles and relevant circuit guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No per se or categorical joint-employer findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final rule intends to treat general contractors in the construction industry—or any entities—as joint employers on a per se or categorical basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entities must meet all elements of the standard in individual cases rather than being classified as joint employers by industry or category alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification/recusal standard for rulemaking participants
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual should be disqualified from rulemaking only when there has been a 'clear and convincing showing' that the official 'has an unalterably closed mind on matters critical to the disposition of the proceeding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive Order 13989 (the Biden Ethics Pledge) does not disqualify Members Wilcox or Prouty here because the rulemaking is not a 'particular matter involving specific parties that is directly and substantially related to' their former employers or clients; the bar for disqualification is therefore high and requires specific proof.
